---
title: "A Poisson regression analysis"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The Nettle language rate model asks whether expected reported language density changes with mean growing season. Recall that the [country count](poisson-regression.qmd#nettle-country-counts) is attached to a geopolitical unit and may include languages that also cross another country's border. Recall also that an [offset](exposure-offsets.qmd) fixes the area coefficient at one, thereby requiring expected count to grow in direct proportion to area.

We ask four questions. Does a longer mean growing season correspond to a different expected language rate? How uncertain is that association under the row independence approximation? Does the Poisson mean--variance relation fit the observed counts? And which claims remain unavailable because countries and reported languages do not form independent biological sampling units?

The fitted Poisson [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) equals its fitted mean. The printed interval uses a row [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) approximation, even though neighboring country records may remain related through geography, history, and documentation practices.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-application
#| echo: true
nettle <- read.csv("data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(nettle) == 74L)
```

The primary model is

$$
Y_i\mid\lambda_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),
\qquad
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

The [Poisson likelihood](poisson-regression.qmd#from-the-count-model-to-the-coefficient-estimates) gives the coefficient estimates and also gives a local measure of their uncertainty. Recall that the Hessian collects the second derivatives of the log likelihood with respect to every pair of coefficients. At the fitted coefficients, its negative is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf I}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T
\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\lambda_1,\ldots,\widehat\lambda_n)
\mathbf X.
$$

This matrix is called the **observed information** because it records the log likelihood's fitted curvature. A sharply curved likelihood changes quickly when a coefficient moves away from its estimate, while a flatter likelihood changes more slowly. Under the model and with enough independent rows, the inverse curvature approximates the sampling covariance of the coefficient estimator:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}
(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
\approx
\widehat{\mathbf I}^{-1}.
$$

The square root of a diagonal entry is the corresponding coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd). Thus an approximate 95% Wald interval for the MGS coefficient is

$$
\widehat\beta_1
\mathbin{\pm}
1.96\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\beta_1).
$$

The coefficient lies on the log rate scale. Exponentiating its estimate gives the fitted multiplicative change in expected languages per square kilometer for one additional month of mean growing season, and exponentiating the two interval endpoints gives the corresponding interval for the rate ratio.

We can now fit the stated model and check the reported standard errors against the inverse curvature calculation. The second fit deliberately inserts base-10 log area into a model whose link uses natural logarithms, allowing us to inspect the consequence of that mismatch.

```{r}
#| label: fit-nettle-application
#| echo: true
correct <- glm(
  language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2),
  poisson(link = "log"),
  nettle
)
mismatched <- glm(
  language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log10_area_km2),
  poisson(link = "log"),
  nettle
)

X <- model.matrix(correct)
observed_information <- crossprod(X, X * fitted(correct))
manual_standard_error <- sqrt(diag(solve(observed_information)))
software_standard_error <- coef(summary(correct))[, "Std. Error"]

standard_error_check <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(correct)),
  manual = manual_standard_error,
  software = software_standard_error,
  difference = manual_standard_error - software_standard_error,
  row.names = NULL
)
standard_error_check
stopifnot(max(abs(standard_error_check$difference)) < 1e-8)

data.frame(
  offset = c("natural log area", "base-10 log area inserted directly"),
  mgs_coefficient = c(coef(correct)[[2L]], coef(mismatched)[[2L]]),
  rate_ratio = exp(c(coef(correct)[[2L]], coef(mismatched)[[2L]]))
)
```

The two standard error calculations agree because both invert the same fitted likelihood curvature. The row independence and Poisson variance assumptions still determine whether the interval has its advertised repeated sampling behavior for these country records.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-rate-ratio-uncertainty
#| echo: true
b <- coef(summary(correct))["mean_growing_season_months", ]
link_interval <- b["Estimate"] + qnorm(c(.025, .975)) * b["Std. Error"]
rate_ratio <- exp(b["Estimate"])
rate_ratio_interval <- exp(link_interval)

mgs_example <- range(nettle$mean_growing_season_months)
common_area_km2 <- median(exp(nettle$log_area_km2))
example_counts <- exp(
  log(common_area_km2) + coef(correct)[[1L]] +
    coef(correct)[[2L]] * mgs_example
)
data.frame(estimate = exp(b["Estimate"]), lower = exp(link_interval[1]),
           upper = exp(link_interval[2]))
```

For one additional month of mean growing season, the fitted language rate per
square kilometer is multiplied by `r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio)`, with a
95% Wald interval under row independence from
`r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio_interval[[1L]])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio_interval[[2L]])`. At the median observed country area
of `r format(round(common_area_km2), big.mark = ",")` square kilometers, the two
observed MGS endpoints, `r sprintf("%.1f", mgs_example[[1L]])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", mgs_example[[2L]])` months give fitted expected counts of
`r sprintf("%.2f", example_counts[[1L]])` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", example_counts[[2L]])`. Their ratio is determined entirely by
the fitted MGS coefficient and the endpoint difference. It describes the model's
country-row association; countries were not assigned to climates, so the
calculation does not identify a causal climate effect.

The mismatch changes the coefficient because it no longer encodes $\lambda_i=A_i r_i$ with an exposure coefficient of one.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-application-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
nettle$observed_rate <- nettle$language_count / exp(nettle$log_area_km2)
grid <- data.frame(mean_growing_season_months =
  seq(min(nettle$mean_growing_season_months),
      max(nettle$mean_growing_season_months), length.out = 200L))
grid$fitted_rate <- exp(coef(correct)[[1L]] + coef(correct)[[2L]] *
                          grid$mean_growing_season_months)
ggplot(nettle, aes(mean_growing_season_months, observed_rate)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = fitted_rate), color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Mean growing season (months)", y = "Languages per square kilometer") +
  theme_classic()
```

The fitted positive association describes the 74 represented country totals under a
fixed area exposure assumption. Country boundaries collect languages, histories,
and documentation practices into one row, while some languages can cross those
boundaries. Countries were not assigned to climates, and the data contain no
intervention that could separate growing season from those other processes.
Nettle's original specification also estimated the area coefficient rather than
fixing it to one.

The Poisson variance restriction should also be checked rather than assumed. Pearson dispersion and the most influential countries diagnose different problems: variance misspecification versus sensitivity to particular design points.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-poisson-checks
#| echo: true
pearson_dispersion <- sum(residuals(correct, type = "pearson")^2) /
  df.residual(correct)
cooks <- cooks.distance(correct)
data.frame(pearson_dispersion,
           most_influential_country = nettle$country[which.max(cooks)],
           maximum_cooks_distance = max(cooks))
```

## Recap and check

1. What happens if base-10 log area is inserted as a natural log offset? The fixed coefficient no longer represents proportional exposure, and the climate estimate changes.
2. Does a positive fitted rate ratio establish a climate effect? No. It is a descriptive association under the distribution, mean, exposure, and independence assumptions.
3. Where does the Wald standard error come from? It is the square root of the relevant diagonal entry in the inverse fitted information matrix.

The [Pearson dispersion ratio](count-overdispersion.qmd) helps us assess whether the counts vary more than the fitted Poisson model permits.
